sections.title: Global Equities
sections.content:
September 2026 delivered a sharply bifurcated global equity tape, with the Federal Reserve's first rate hike since July 2023 and a surge in US Treasury yields to multi-year highs cleaving markets along style, sector, and geographic lines. The Nasdaq Composite defied the macro headwinds to post a **+1.9%** monthly advance to **26,861.06**, propelled almost entirely by AI mega-cap names, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average bore the full weight of rate sensitivity, tumbling **-4.3%** to **50,906.05** — its worst monthly performance of 2026. The S&P 500 split the difference, declining a modest **-0.5%** to **7,651.54**, with its significant technology weighting providing partial insulation against the broader selloff.

European bourses navigated a challenging backdrop of a stronger dollar and re-accelerating energy costs, with the DAX closing September near **25,199** (approx., verify before merging) and the FTSE 100 settling around **10,606** (approx., verify before merging). In APAC, Japan's Nikkei 225 advanced to approximately **66,754** (approx., verify before merging) as the Bank of Japan's rate hike to a **31-year high** of **1.25%** was interpreted constructively by equity investors, while Chinese indices remained pressured by oil-import cost inflation and sluggish domestic demand.

sections.title: Your Must-Know Market Themes
sections.content: Four key themes that shaped markets this month:
themes:
Fed Resumes Rate-Hike Cycle After Three-Year Pause -- The singular catalyst of September 2026 was the FOMC's unanimous **12-0** vote on September 16 to raise the federal funds target range by **25 basis points** to **3.75%–4.00%** — the first rate increase since July 2023 and the end of the longest rate-hold period in the current cycle. Fed Chair Kevin Warsh cited persistent upside inflation risks, a resilient labour market, and oil-driven cost pressures as the primary justifications; markets had priced better than **90%** odds of the hike in advance, but the hawkish accompanying guidance — signalling at least one additional **25bps** move by year-end — delivered a further shock to rate expectations. The dot-plot update pointed to a median terminal rate of **4.1%** by end-2026.

The transmission through financial markets was immediate and severe. The 10-year Treasury yield breached **5.00%** intraday — its highest level since **2007** — and the DXY index staged its strongest monthly rally since June. Rate-sensitive equity sectors sold off sharply, with REITs, utilities, and regional banks leading declines, and the equal-weight S&P 500 underperforming its cap-weighted counterpart by approximately **450 basis points** for the month. The Fed's return to tightening represents a fundamental reassessment of the risk-free rate backdrop for global asset valuations entering Q4 2026.

Oil Surge Rekindles Global Inflation Premium -- Crude oil was the other dominant market force of the month, with Brent rallying approximately **+10.8%** in September — breaching the psychologically significant **$100/bbl** level for the first time since early 2025 — while WTI gained approximately **+7.6%** in parallel. The move reflected OPEC+ supply discipline, Middle East geopolitical risk premium, and stronger-than-expected US demand data through the summer. US CPI was running at **3.4%** year-over-year through August, and the oil re-acceleration threatened to push headline readings materially higher into year-end.

For central banks already navigating a complex dual-mandate trade-off, the oil shock was deeply unwelcome. The ECB and Bank of England — both caught between slowing industrial activity and energy-driven cost pressures — faced the spectre of a 2022-style stagflationary dynamic. The gold market responded in a structurally unusual fashion: bullion declined approximately **-6.6%** in September as the very oil-driven inflation surge that would traditionally support it instead reinforced the case for Fed tightening, lifting real yields and the dollar simultaneously — both structural headwinds for non-yielding precious metals.

AI Mega-Cap Bifurcation Rescues the Nasdaq -- Tech-driven index divergence reached an extreme in September, with the Nasdaq Composite gaining **+1.9%** to **26,861.06** while the Dow Jones Industrial Average tumbled **-4.3%** to **50,906.05** — a spread of nearly **630 basis points** between two headline US indices. The bifurcation was concentrated almost entirely in the AI infrastructure and semiconductor complex: AMD surged approximately **9%** in a single session to cross the **$1 trillion** market cap threshold for the first time, while the broader Magnificent 7 cohort hit intraday all-time highs as a group. Big Tech's aggregate AI capital expenditure commitment reached approximately **$405 billion**, with Q3 spending up an estimated **75%** year-over-year.

The outperformance of AI-exposed growth names over the broader market reflected a structural repositioning dynamic: as bond yields surged, duration-sensitive value and cyclical names sold off, while high-multiple AI growers were sustained by earnings momentum and the market's willingness to look through higher discount rates given the pace of top-line acceleration. Nvidia's revenue continued to grow approximately **100%** year-over-year, underpinning premium valuations. The extraordinary leadership concentration raises medium-term breadth concerns, but AI earnings delivery has so far provided fundamental justification for the divergence.

Bank of Japan Hikes to 31-Year High, Yen Paradox Unfolds -- The Bank of Japan's September 18 decision to raise its policy rate by **25 basis points** to **1.25%** — the highest level since **1995** — was executed against a backdrop of rising domestic inflation and coordinated US-Japan currency management discussions. Governor Kazuo Ueda characterised the decision as marking a "new policy phase," but the **7-2** split vote, the absence of updated economic forecasts, and his non-committal guidance on future hikes produced a notably muted hawkish transmission in FX markets. The yen paradoxically weakened past **¥157** per dollar despite the hike, and the Nikkei 225 rose approximately **1.5%** on the day of the decision.

The yen's counter-intuitive post-hike weakness reflected the market's judgment that the BOJ's incremental approach remained far behind the curve relative to Fed tightening, leaving the US-Japan interest-rate differential still strongly in the dollar's favour at approximately **250 basis points**. Export-oriented Japanese corporates benefited directly from the sustained yen weakness, supporting Nikkei outperformance with the index approaching **66,754** (approx., verify before merging) by month-end. A further BOJ hike is pencilled in for December, but cautious guidance has shifted the trajectory lower, placing currency dynamics rather than domestic monetary policy normalisation as the dominant variable for Japanese markets in Q4.

sections.title: US Equities
sections.content:
US equity markets delivered a net negative tape in September, with the S&P 500 declining **-0.5%** to close at **7,651.54** and the Dow Jones Industrial Average shedding **-4.3%** to **50,906.05** — its worst monthly performance of 2026. The Federal Reserve's September 16 rate hike — unanimous and accompanied by hawkish forward guidance projecting the funds rate reaching **4.1%** by year-end — acted as the primary catalyst for a violent rotation out of rate-sensitive sectors as investors rapidly repriced the interest-rate outlook following five consecutive hold decisions.

The Nasdaq Composite was the notable outlier, gaining **+1.9%** to close at **26,861.06**, as AI-exposed megacap technology names proved largely immune to the rate headwind. AMD surged approximately **9%** in a single session to briefly breach a **$1 trillion** market capitalisation, the Magnificent 7 ETF hit intraday all-time highs, and Nvidia continued to trade at elevated multiples supported by revenue growth of approximately **100%** year-over-year. Sector dispersion was extreme: technology and communication services posted gains while real estate, utilities, and financials — adversely affected by higher yields or compressed margins — logged sharp losses.

The month's narrow tape reinforced the dominant 2026 equity cycle theme: AI megacap quality provides a resilient index-level floor, but breadth beneath the surface remained dangerously thin. The equal-weight S&P 500 underperformed its cap-weighted counterpart by approximately **450 basis points** for the month — a degree of concentration that elevates idiosyncratic risk heading into the Q3 earnings season in October.

sections.title: European Equities
sections.content:
European equity markets faced a challenging September, caught between a resurgent dollar, elevated energy import costs, and the global repricing of rate expectations that followed the Fed's hawkish pivot. The DAX closed September near **25,199** (approx., verify before merging), the CAC 40 settled around **7,957** (approx., verify before merging), and the FTSE 100 retreated to approximately **10,606** (approx., verify before merging). Energy-importing economies faced particular headwinds as Brent crude surged above **$100/bbl** for the first time since early 2025, lifting input cost pressures across manufacturing and transportation sectors.

The European Central Bank maintained its deposit rate at **2.50%** following its June hike, but policymakers grew increasingly attentive to oil-driven second-round inflation effects. Eurozone industrial production remained subdued against a backdrop of weak Chinese demand and ongoing competitive pressures from Asian manufacturers. UK equities underperformed on a relative basis as the Bank of England held Bank Rate at **3.75%** on a narrow **6-3** vote, signalling internal division over the inflation-growth trade-off and leaving sterling without a clear policy tailwind.

The structural bifurcation within European markets sharpened in September: FTSE 100 energy and mining heavyweights benefited from crude's advance, while rate-sensitive continental sectors — property, utilities, and domestic financials — faced meaningful headwinds from the global yield surge. European sovereign yields rose in lockstep with Treasuries, and Italian BTP spreads versus German Bunds widened modestly, reintroducing peripheral risk considerations for eurozone fixed income positioning.

sections.title: APAC Equities
sections.content:
Japan delivered the standout APAC equity performance in September. The Nikkei 225 closed the month near **66,754** (approx., verify before merging), recovering from mid-month volatility around the Bank of Japan's rate hike decision to finish with healthy gains supported by export-oriented corporates, semiconductor names, and the continued AI-investment thematic. The BOJ's move to **1.25%** — the highest policy rate since **1995** — was interpreted as a signal of genuine economic confidence rather than destabilising tightening; paradoxically, the yen weakened past **¥157** post-decision, directly benefiting exporters. Japan's year-to-date equity gains remained among the strongest in developed markets, standing at approximately **+29%** through September.

Chinese equity markets faced a more difficult month. The Shanghai Composite closed near **3,842** (approx., verify before merging), weighed down by surging oil import costs, a stronger dollar tightening EM financial conditions, and persistent uncertainty around the property sector recovery. The Hang Seng Index hovered near **25,087** (approx., verify before merging) by month-end as Hong Kong-listed names — carrying greater sensitivity to global risk sentiment and foreign capital flows — were caught in the crossfire of macro deterioration.

The APAC divergence in September — Japan resilient while Chinese markets declined — reflects fundamentally different macroeconomic trajectories. Japan is experiencing wage-driven inflation that validates BOJ normalisation, while China faces an external terms-of-trade shock from higher oil and a domestic demand environment running below trend. This contrast creates a meaningful intra-regional allocation debate, and the divergence appears likely to persist into Q4 absent a material commodity price reversal or significant targeted fiscal stimulus from Beijing.

sections.title: Foreign Exchange
sections.content:
The US Dollar Index (DXY) advanced approximately **+2.0%** in September to close near **101.45** — its strongest monthly performance since June — as two powerful dollar-bullish forces converged: the Fed's hawkish pivot delivering its first rate hike since 2023 and broad safe-haven demand driven by Middle East geopolitical escalation. The advance was wide-ranging across major currency pairs, with the euro and sterling both suffering meaningful declines.

EUR/USD fell approximately **-2.25%** to close near **1.14**, as the ECB's decision to hold rates at **2.50%** while the Fed resumed tightening materially widened the transatlantic yield differential in the dollar's favour; European growth concerns amplified the move. GBP/USD declined approximately **-1.90%** to around **1.33**, with sterling constrained by the Bank of England's uncertain policy path and the UK's elevated sensitivity to energy import costs. USD/JPY settled near **157.00** (approx., verify before merging) by month-end following the BOJ's September 18 hike to **1.25%**, though the pair's exact monthly directional move remains disputed across primary data sources due to the impact of coordinated US-Japan currency interventions conducted in the lead-up to the decision.

The FX dynamics of September crystallised a key macro thesis: the dollar's trajectory is increasingly shaped not just by relative rate differentials but by the geopolitical oil shock and its asymmetric impact on current account balances. Oil-importing economies — Europe, Japan, South Korea, and China — face structurally weaker currencies unless their central banks respond with matching rate increases, creating a differentiated FX landscape that rewards policy-normalising central banks and penalises those still in pause mode entering Q4.

sections.title: Commodities
sections.content:
Crude oil was the defining commodity story of September, with Brent surging approximately **+10.8%** and WTI climbing approximately **+7.6%** as Middle East supply-disruption fears, OPEC+ production discipline, and US inventory draws converged into a powerful upside catalyst. Brent breached the psychologically significant **$100/bbl** level during the month — a critical juncture for global inflation trajectories — and traded near **$109/bbl** by mid-October (approx., verify before merging). The oil advance was the largest single monthly gain in crude since 2022 and will add measurably to global headline CPI readings through Q4.

Gold moved inversely and sharply, declining approximately **-6.6%** in September as the very oil-driven inflation surge that would traditionally support bullion instead reinforced the case for Fed tightening, lifting real yields and the DXY simultaneously — both structural headwinds for non-yielding precious metals. The metal fell toward approximately **$4,150/oz** by month-end (approx., verify before merging), having traded near **$4,290/oz** ahead of the September 16 Fed decision. Industrial copper edged lower by roughly **-1.0%**, a modest pullback relative to its August record high of **$6.96/lb**, reflecting demand uncertainty from slowing Chinese manufacturing activity and a stronger dollar weighing on commodity prices broadly.

The commodity landscape heading into Q4 presents a challenging policy dilemma: oil structurally above **$90/bbl** sustains persistent headline CPI pressure globally, while gold's proximity to all-time highs despite the monthly pullback signals sustained institutional appetite for macro hedges. The divergence between energy outperformance and precious metals weakness reflects the market's interpretation that this commodity cycle is primarily geopolitically and supply-constrained rather than demand-driven — a distinction with important implications for how central banks interpret the resulting inflationary signal.

sections.title: Fixed Income
sections.content:
September was among the most consequential months for bond markets in recent memory. The FOMC's unanimous September 16 rate hike to a target range of **3.75%–4.00%** — the first increase since July 2023 — catalysed a violent repricing across the Treasury curve, with the 10-year US yield surging above **5.00%** on the day of the decision, its highest print since **2007**. By September 25, the benchmark 10-year had settled near **5.17%** and the 2-year note near **4.81%**, compressing the 10s-2s spread to approximately **36 basis points** in a tentative bear steepening consistent with markets pricing structurally higher long-run neutral rates.

Three concurrent forces drove the velocity and breadth of the sell-off: the Fed's hawkish policy pivot, the inflationary signal from oil crossing **$100/bbl** during the month with CPI running at **3.4%** year-over-year through August, and growing investor concern over US fiscal sustainability requiring structurally higher term premia. Chair Warsh's post-meeting commentary explicitly referenced persistent energy-driven cost pressures, and the dot-plot median projecting the funds rate at **4.1%** by end-2026 implied at least one additional hike in Q4, with markets pricing a meaningful probability of a December move. The 30-year Treasury yield was reported near multi-decade highs not seen since the early 2000s.

Globally, developed-market government bonds sold off in sympathy with Treasuries: UK Gilt yields rose sharply, German Bund yields tested levels that complicated ECB credibility, and peripheral eurozone spreads widened as higher global rates pressured weaker sovereign credits. Municipal bonds and mortgage-backed securities sold off in sympathy, with 30-year average US mortgage rates climbing above **7.23%** and renewing pressure on the housing market. September's duration drawdown was the largest single-month loss for long-dated bonds in 2026, reinforcing the case for short-duration and barbell positioning ahead of a potentially further-hawkish Q4 Fed.
